items.title: Complying with consumer law when using AI agents
items.locator: Sections 'Tell your customers if you use an AI agent' and 'When it comes to dealing with your customers, the same rules apply whether using AI or human agents'
items.why: Source of the quotation. Also says the business is responsible for an AI agent as for an employee, even where someone else designed or provides it, and that fines can reach 10% of worldwide turnover. Published 9 March 2026. Guidance, not statute: it says 'consider whether you need to label it'.
items.quote: you are responsible for what an AI agent does in the same way you are responsible for what an employee does

items.title: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024, section 227: Misleading omissions
items.why: The legal test behind the guidance. Material information is what the average consumer needs to take an informed transactional decision; information given so the consumer is unlikely to see it counts as omitted. In force 6 April 2025 (S.I. 2025/272). The section does not mention AI.
items.quote: information that the average consumer needs to take an informed transactional decision

items.title: AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689), Article 50: Transparency obligations for providers and deployers of certain AI systems
items.publisher: European Commission, AI Act Service Desk
items.locator: Article 50(1) and 50(5); application date from Article 113 on the same site
items.why: The explicit duty, placed on providers, with the 'obvious' exception and the 'at the latest at the time of the first interaction' rule. This is the Commission's copy, not the Official Journal (EUR-Lex returned empty pages). The page carries a notice that the provision has been amended by the Digital Omnibus on AI and the text is not yet updated; the amendment marker sits on paragraph 7, not paragraph 1.
items.quote: the natural persons concerned are informed that they are interacting with an AI system

items.title: Guidelines on the implementation of the transparency obligations for certain AI systems under Article 50 of the AI Act, C(2026) 5054 final, Annex
items.why: Says disclosure only in terms and conditions is insufficient (para 38), the exception 'should be interpreted restrictively' (para 45), and helpdesk chatbots do not qualify as obvious (p. 18). Non-binding (para 5). Content approved 20 July 2026; the covering communication says formal adoption follows once all language versions exist. The landing page states that Article 50 applies from 2 August 2026.
items.quote: These transparency obligations apply from 2 August 2026.

items.title: A pro-innovation approach to AI regulation (white paper)
items.publisher: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
items.locator: Paragraphs 10-11; section 3.2.3, 'Principle: Appropriate transparency and explainability'
items.why: Lists the five principles and says they are issued on a non-statutory basis. Defines transparency as communicating 'how, when, and for which purposes an AI system is being used'. Published under the previous government; no later statement of the principles was read in this pass.
items.quote: information on how, when, and for which purposes an AI system is being used

items.title: Should AI systems behave like people?
items.publisher: AI Security Institute (then AI Safety Institute)
items.locator: Section on transparency, first bullet; survey description above it; Figure 1 caption
items.why: Source of the figure (68% agreed, 16% disagreed). Survey with Deltapoll, March 2024. The text gives a sample of 1,583 UK adults; the caption to Figure 1 gives 1,498 respondents for these questions. A blog post, not a full report.
items.quote: 68% agreed that it should be made clear whether the agent was human or artificial, whereas only 16% disagreed

items.title: OECD AI Principles: Transparency and explainability (Principle 1.3)
items.quote: to make stakeholders aware of their interactions with AI systems, including in the workplace
items.why: International comparator. The intergovernmental principle asks AI actors to make people aware they are dealing with AI, and extends it to the workplace, which the UK consumer-law route does not. The OECD's own page for the principle; the legal instrument itself (OECD/LEGAL/0449) could not be read because its site needs JavaScript, and the page shows no adoption or revision date. A non-binding recommendation to governments, not a rule for firms. Year is that of first adoption, from background knowledge.

items.title: Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence
items.locator: Paragraph 127 (policy area on communication and information / human-AI interaction); see also paragraph 38, last sentence
items.quote: users can easily identify whether they are interacting with a living being, or with an AI system imitating human or animal characteristics
items.why: The global standard adopted by UNESCO's General Conference. Paragraph 127 adds a right to refuse the interaction and ask for a person; paragraph 38 says users should be told when a service is provided with AI. Addressed to states, non-binding, and written before generative chatbots were common.

items.title: Model Artificial Intelligence Governance Framework, Second Edition
items.publisher: Infocomm Media Development Authority and Personal Data Protection Commission, Singapore
items.quote: an online portal may inform its users that they are interacting with an AI-powered chatbot and not a human customer service agent
items.why: Comparator from Singapore: a regulator-issued, voluntary framework that treats disclosure of a chatbot as the basic example of general disclosure. Voluntary ('encouraged'), dated 2020 and not updated for generative AI in this edition.

items.title: California Business and Professions Code, section 17941 (Bots)
items.locator: s.17941(a) and (b); added by Stats. 2018, Ch. 892 (SB 1001), operative 1 July 2019
items.quote: A person using a bot shall not be liable under this section if the person discloses that it is a bot.
items.why: The earliest statute found that makes disclosure the safe harbour. Narrower than it is often described: it bites only where a bot is used with intent to mislead in order to sell goods or services or influence a vote. Disclosure must be 'clear, conspicuous, and reasonably designed'. US state law, no effect in the UK.

items.title: California Senate Bill No. 243 (Companion chatbots), Chapter 677, Statutes of 2025
items.locator: Section 1, adding Business and Professions Code s.22602(a)
items.quote: an operator shall issue a clear and conspicuous notification indicating that the companion chatbot is artificially generated and not human
items.why: A 2025 statute that uses a reasonable-person test close to the EU's 'obvious' exception: notification is owed where a reasonable person would be misled into thinking they are talking to a human. Covers companion chatbots only. Chaptered bill text; the operative date and any later amendment were not checked. US state law.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Playbook for the UK Government
items.locator: Principle 7: You are open and collaborative
items.quote: You should also clearly identify any automated response to the public.
items.why: The UK government's own standard for public bodies, with example wording for a chatbot reply ('this response has been written by an automated AI chatbot'). Guidance for the public sector, not a duty on companies; useful as a benchmark for what 'exceeds the legal floor' looks like in the UK.

items.title: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024, section 226: Misleading actions
items.quote: an overall presentation which is likely to deceive the average consumer about a matter relating to a product, a trader or any other matter
items.why: The second consumer-law route alongside misleading omissions: an agent presented so that people take it for a person can deceive by overall presentation even if nothing false is said. The section does not mention AI; applying it to chatbots is a reading of the CMA's guidance, not a court ruling.

items.title: Frontiers: Machines vs. Humans: The Impact of Artificial Intelligence Chatbot Disclosure on Customer Purchases
items.publisher: Luo, Tong, Fang and Qu, Marketing Science 38(6)
items.quote: reduces purchase rates by more than 79.7%
items.why: Peer-reviewed field experiment on more than 6,200 customers: disclosing the chatbot before an outbound sales call cut purchases sharply. Shows the commercial incentive not to disclose, which is why a written standard is needed. A single firm's structured outbound sales calls, with 2019 technology; the copy read is hosted by the lead author's university (Temple), and the journal's own site was not read.

items.title: Trust me, I'm a bot: repercussions of chatbot disclosure in different service frontline settings
items.publisher: Mozafari, Weiger and Hammerschmidt, Journal of Service Management
items.quote: Chatbot disclosure has a negative indirect effect on customer retention through mitigated trust for services with high criticality.
items.why: Peer-reviewed. Two scenario experiments: disclosure costs trust where the service matters a great deal, but helps retention when the chatbot fails to solve the problem. Supports user-testing the wording and placement instead of assuming disclosure is neutral. Simulated interactions, not live customers; copy hosted by the authors' university (Goettingen).

items.title: Large Language Models Pass the Turing Test
items.quote: GPT-4.5 was judged to be the human 73% of the time
items.why: Why silence now deceives: in pre-registered three-party tests, people picked a prompted language model as the human more often than the real person. Weakens any reliance on the interaction being 'obvious'. Preprint, not peer reviewed on the date checked; five-minute text chats in two participant pools.
